heroIntro: Discovering that a civil court has passed an ex-parte decree against you without your knowledge is one of the most alarming crises in Bangladeshi property litigation. Whether engineered by unscrupulous relatives or predatory land grabbers through forged summons receipts, the Code of Civil Procedure provides robust, enforceable remedies to set aside one-sided judgments and restore your lawful defense.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: How to Cancel an Ex-Parte Decree in Bangladesh
quickAnswer.text: Under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC), an aggrieved defendant can file a Miscellaneous Case in the trial court to set aside an ex-parte decree by proving that the court summons was never duly served or that they were prevented by sufficient cause from attending. If the decree was obtained through deliberate fraud, an application under Section 12(2) CPC can be instituted to declare the decree void ab initio.

sections.title: The Crisis of Ex-Parte Decrees in Bangladesh
sections.content:
Imagine living abroad as an expatriate wage earner in London, New York, or Riyadh, diligently sending remittances home to build your family homestead, only to receive a panicked telephone call from your ancestral village in Sylhet or Cumilla. A court bailiff has appeared on your land with police personnel, preparing to execute a writ of possession based on an ex-parte civil decree that you had no idea ever existed.

This distressing scenario occurs frequently across the subordinate judiciary of Bangladesh. Dishonest co-sharers, estranged relatives, or predatory land syndicates intentionally file partition suits, title declarations, or specific performance claims while suppressing the defendant's genuine overseas or urban address. By bribing local process servers to submit fictitious service returns or publishing court notices in obscure, uncirculated daily gazettes, plaintiffs secure one-sided judgments behind the defendant's back.

Acknowledge your anxiety, but understand that the judicial system does not allow fraudulent or uninformed decrees to stand unchecked. The Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC) enshrines the fundamental common-law maxim of natural justice: audi alteram partem (no person shall be condemned unheard). With aggressive and prompt legal intervention, an ex-parte decree can be reopened, execution halted, and your rightful defense placed fully before the trial court.

sections.title: Statutory Framework: Order IX Rule 13 CPC Explained
sections.content:
Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 serves as the principal statutory shield for any defendant subjected to a unilateral civil decree. The rule explicitly provides that in any case where a decree is passed ex-parte against a defendant, that defendant may apply to the court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside.

If the applicant satisfies the court of either of two statutory conditions—first, that the summons was not duly served, or second, that they were prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing—the court is statutorily mandated to make an order setting aside the decree as against them. The court may impose such terms as to costs, payment into court, or otherwise as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the original suit.

When an ex-parte decree is set aside under Order IX Rule 13, the judicial clock is wound backward. The decree is extinguished, and the original lawsuit is restored to its status prior to the default. The defendant is granted full legal standing to submit a Written Statement (WS), introduce documentary evidence, cross-examine the plaintiff's witnesses, and contest the merits on an equal footing.

sections.title: Grounds: Summons Not Duly Served vs. Sufficient Cause
sections.content:
To succeed in an application under Order IX Rule 13, the applicant must establish at least one of the two statutory grounds recognized under Bangladeshi civil jurisprudence:

  • Summons Not Duly Served: Under Order V of the CPC, the court must serve summons through personal delivery, registered post with acknowledgment due (A/D), or courier. If the plaintiff provided a deliberately false address, if the process server (Jari-karak) submitted a fraudulent return without visiting the locality, or if substituted service under Order V Rule 20 (hanging on a door or publishing in an obscure newspaper) was granted without genuine efforts to trace the defendant, the summons is legally invalid.
  • Sufficient Cause for Non-Appearance: Even if summons was served, the defendant may have been physically or legally unable to appear on the date of hearing. Bangladeshi courts recognize severe illness certified by government medical boards, sudden bereavement, confinement in foreign jurisdictions, inability to travel due to visa cancellation, or proven gross fraud by engaged legal counsel as sufficient cause.

Judges require credible contemporaneous documentation to substantiate sufficient cause. Mere assertions of busyness or casual ignorance of court dates will be rejected by the bench.

sections.title: Section 12(2) CPC: Decrees Procured by Fraud or Collusion
sections.content:
While Order IX Rule 13 addresses procedural absence and service irregularities, what happens when an ex-parte decree was manufactured through deep-seated criminal fraud, forged deeds, or impersonation? In such severe instances, Section 12(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure represents the definitive constitutional remedy.

Introduced to prevent endless rounds of independent title suits, Section 12(2) provides that where a person challenges the validity of a decree, judgment, or order on the ground of fraud, misrepresentation, or want of jurisdiction, they must seek their remedy by making an application to the court which passed the final decree, rather than filing a separate lawsuit.

The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly affirmed that fraud vitiates the most solemn judicial acts. If a plaintiff forged the signature of a deceased ancestor, fabricated a power of attorney, or deliberately impersonated the defendant through a hired imposter in court, an application under Section 12(2) enables the trial court to exercise its inherent supervisory jurisdiction, annul the fraudulent decree, and refer the perpetrators for criminal prosecution under Sections 193, 209, and 467 of the Penal Code.

sections.title: Strict Limitation Deadlines: Article 164 Limitation Act
sections.content:
Timing is the most perilous dimension of ex-parte litigation in Bangladesh. Under Article 164 of the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory period to file an application under Order IX Rule 13 to set aside an ex-parte decree is strictly 30 days.

However, the crucial question is when this 30-day countdown begins:

  • Where Summons Was Duly Served: The 30 days run from the exact date of the decree.
  • Where Summons Was Not Duly Served: The 30 days run from the date when the applicant first acquired knowledge of the decree.

If you discover an ex-parte decree months or years after its pronouncement because you were living abroad or unserved, you must document precisely how and when you first learned of the judgment (e.g., when a relative saw strangers inspecting the land, or when mutation was attempted). You must immediately file an accompanying application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act 1908, praying for condonation of delay and explaining every single day between gaining knowledge and filing the petition in court.

sections.title: Staying the Execution Case: Order XXI and Order XXXIX
sections.content:
Filing an application to set aside an ex-parte decree does not automatically prevent the plaintiff from taking possession of your land. In practice, the victorious plaintiff immediately files a Money Execution Case or Title Execution Case (Jari Mamla) under Order XXI of the CPC to obtain a writ of delivery of possession (Dakhol Parwana) or auction your properties.

Therefore, your legal counsel must file an urgent application for an interim stay of execution proceedings concurrently with your Order IX Rule 13 petition:

  1. Order XXI Rule 26 CPC: Empowers the execution court to stay the execution of a decree for a reasonable time to enable the judgment-debtor to apply to the trial court or appellate court for an order setting aside the decree.
  2. Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2 CPC: Allows the court hearing the Miscellaneous Case to issue a temporary injunction restraining the opposite party from altering the nature, character, or possession of the suit property during the pendency of the hearing.
  3. Inherent Powers under Section 151 CPC: Invoked where technical procedural gaps exist, empowering the civil judge to pass ad-interim status-quo orders in the interest of justice.

Without securing an interim stay order, the plaintiff may demolish existing structures, fell timber, or convey the land to an alleged innocent third party, creating severe practical complications.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Miscellaneous Case Procedure in Court
sections.content:
Challenging an ex-parte decree follows a rigorous, multi-stage judicial pathway in the subordinate civil courts of Bangladesh:

  1. Procuring Certified Copies: Apply urgently for certified copies of the ex-parte judgment, decree, order sheet, and crucially, the process server's summons return (Jarikar report) from the court record room.
  2. Drafting the Miscellaneous Application: Your advocate drafts a formal petition under Order IX Rule 13 (and Section 151) CPC, detailing the jurisdictional facts, non-service of summons, and substantial defense on the merits, supported by a verifying affidavit.
  3. Registration as a Misc Case: The civil court admits the petition, registering it as an independent Miscellaneous Case (Misc Case) and assigning it a unique case number.
  4. Notice to the Opposite Party: Summons is issued to the original plaintiff, who is granted time to submit written objections.
  5. Evidentiary Hearing (Hearing on Evidence): Both parties produce oral and documentary evidence. The applicant testifies under oath, and the process server who claimed to have served the summons can be summoned and rigorously cross-examined regarding local identification witnesses.
  6. Final Order and Terms: The civil judge pronounces an order either dismissing the Misc Case or setting aside the ex-parte decree, often imposing moderate court costs (BDT 1,000 to BDT 5,000) payable to the plaintiff.

sections.title: Comparison Table: Order IX Rule 13 vs. Section 12(2) CPC
sections.content:
Choosing the correct procedural vehicle between Order IX Rule 13 and Section 12(2) CPC determines whether your case survives preliminary judicial scrutiny:

Legal ParameterOrder IX Rule 13 CPCSection 12(2) CPC
Primary GroundNon-service of summons or sufficient cause for absence.Fraud, misrepresentation, or lack of territorial/pecuniary jurisdiction.
ApplicabilityEx-parte decrees only.Any decree, whether ex-parte, contested, or Solenama (compromise).
Statutory LimitationStrictly 30 days under Article 164 Limitation Act (from decree or knowledge).Governed by Article 181 (3 years from discovery of fraud).
Standard of ProofPreponderance of probabilities regarding absence or non-service.High civil standard proving intentional fraudulent deception or forgery.
Immediate ConsequenceRestores the original suit to the trial docket for a fresh hearing.Declares the decree void ab initio, nullifying all execution proceedings.
Right of AppealAppealable under Order XLIII Rule 1(d) CPC to District Judge Court.Civil Revision under Section 115 CPC to District Judge or High Court.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Overturning a Fraudulent Partition Decree
sections.content:
Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): Tariqul, an expatriate software architect working in Birmingham, owned an undivided 12-decimal commercial land parcel along the Sylhet-Sunamganj highway, inherited from his late father. In mid-2025, his paternal uncle filed a Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) in the Joint District Judge Court, intentionally stating Tariqul's address as a defunct village tea stall in Jagannathpur where Tariqul had not lived in thirty years.

The process server allegedly pinned the summons to the vacant shop wall, certifying that the defendant could not be found. Following formal paper publication in a weekly periodical with negligible circulation, the court proceeded ex-parte and decreed the entire roadside commercial frontage to the uncle, relegating Tariqul's share to an unviable waterlogged ditch behind the property.

When Tariqul's maternal cousin noticed boundary fencing being erected in October 2026, Tariqul immediately granted an attested Special Power of Attorney through the Bangladesh High Commission in London to his advocate. His counsel obtained certified copies of the summons return, which bore the forged thumb impression of a fictitious village elder. Within 14 days of knowledge, an Order IX Rule 13 application accompanied by a Section 5 limitation petition and an Order XXI Rule 26 stay application was filed.

During the evidentiary hearing, the process server crumbled under cross-examination, admitting he never verified Tariqul's physical presence. The Joint District Judge set aside the ex-parte partition decree, issued an injunction against construction, and restored the original partition suit, allowing Tariqul to demand an equitable court-appointed Advocate Commissioner survey.

faqs.q: What happens to the original lawsuit when an ex-parte decree is set aside?
faqs.a: When the trial court sets aside an ex-parte decree under Order IX Rule 13 CPC, the decree is completely nullified and the original lawsuit is restored to the exact procedural stage it was at prior to the defendant being declared absent. The defendant is permitted to file their written statement, submit documents, and contest the case on full merits.

faqs.q: How do I prove that I never received the court summons?
faqs.a: Non-service of summons is proven by examining the certified process server report (Jarikar report). Your advocate will inspect the alleged signatures or thumb impressions of local witnesses, cross-examine the process server in court, and submit documentary proof (such as passport stamps, airline tickets, or employment records) showing you resided elsewhere or abroad when service was allegedly made.

faqs.q: Can an expatriate (NRB) apply to set aside an ex-parte decree from abroad?
faqs.a: Yes. An expatriate living abroad can execute a Special Power of Attorney empowering a trusted relative or their advocate in Bangladesh to file and pursue the Order IX Rule 13 Miscellaneous Case. The power of attorney must be duly signed, verified by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, and stamped by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) in Dhaka.

faqs.q: What is the time limit to file an Order IX Rule 13 application?
faqs.a: Under Article 164 of the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory time limit is strictly 30 days. If summons was duly served, the 30 days run from the date of the decree; if summons was not served, the 30 days run from the date the applicant first gained knowledge of the decree, supported by a Section 5 condonation petition.

faqs.q: What if the plaintiff has already sold the property after obtaining the ex-parte decree?
faqs.a: Under the legal doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52 Transfer of Property Act 1882), any third-party purchaser who buys property subject to an ex-parte decree does so at their own peril. When the ex-parte decree is set aside, the subsequent transfer loses its legal foundation, and the property can be recovered through restitution proceedings under Section 144 CPC.

faqs.q: Can the court impose costs or financial conditions when setting aside an ex-parte decree?
faqs.a: Yes. Order IX Rule 13 CPC explicitly empowers the civil judge to set aside the decree 'upon such terms as to costs, payment into court, or otherwise as it thinks fit.' Courts routinely direct the applicant to pay nominal costs (BDT 1,000 to BDT 5,000) to compensate the plaintiff for procedural delays.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Order IX Rule 13 and an appeal under Section 96(2) CPC?
faqs.a: An aggrieved defendant has two concurrent remedies: filing an application under Order IX Rule 13 in the trial court or preferring a regular First Appeal under Section 96(2) CPC before the appellate court. Order IX Rule 13 is vastly preferable because it allows the introduction of fresh evidence regarding non-service of summons, whereas an appeal is confined strictly to the existing trial court paper book.

faqs.q: Can an ex-parte decree in an Artha Rin Adalat or Family Court case be set aside under Order IX Rule 13?
faqs.a: Both Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 and Family Courts Act 2023 have specialized provisions mirroring Order IX Rule 13. However, under Section 19 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003, setting aside an ex-parte money decree requires the judgment-debtor to deposit 10% of the decreed amount in cash or bank guarantee within 30 days of knowledge.
